query: Many physical and chemical fabrication approaches have produced multi-element, near-equiatomic solid-solution nanoparticles, yet their synthesis–structure–property relationships remain poorly established. This limits evaluation of their suitability for catalytic operation at 773–1173 K and thermoelectric use at 473–1923 K, including catalytic settings where low noble-metal content is desirable. What governs whether these nanoparticles preserve structural and chemical stability under such service regimes, and why? Formulate one testable mechanistic hypothesis, specify a controlled intervention that separates it from competing explanations, predict observations relative to a baseline, define its boundary conditions, connect it to the prior evidence summarized above, and provide a clear falsification test.

generation.hypothesis: The high-temperature stability of near‐equiatomic, multi‐element nanoparticles is governed by the combined effects of high configurational entropy and severe lattice distortion. These features kinetically inhibit atomic diffusion and phase segregation, thereby preserving the solid‐solution structure and surface composition—even when noble metals are present at low levels.
generation.material_initial_state: Well‐mixed, near‐equiatomic solid‐solution nanoparticles with a random distribution of elements (e.g., HEA nanoparticles) and pronounced lattice distortion due to atomic size differences.
generation.intervention: Systematically vary the compositional ratios to modulate the atomic size mismatch and thus the degree of lattice distortion (and hence configurational entropy). Compare nanoparticles with maximized mismatch (high lattice distortion) to those with reduced mismatch while holding other synthesis conditions constant.
generation.conditions: Expose both sets of nanoparticles to service-relevant high temperatures (773–1173 K for catalytic and 473–1923 K for thermoelectric applications) under inert or controlled atmospheres to minimize extrinsic oxidation effects.
generation.structural_mediator: Severe lattice distortion arising from significant differences in the sizes of constituent atoms.
generation.mechanism: The severe lattice distortion increases the energy barriers for atomic diffusion, and the high configurational entropy stabilizes the disordered solid-solution phase. Together, these factors slow or prevent phase segregation and coarsening at elevated temperatures, maintaining chemical and structural integrity.
generation.predicted_outcome: Nanoparticles with high atomic size mismatch (and thus maximized configurational entropy and lattice distortion) will show reduced structural coarsening, limited elemental segregation, and better retention of their surface catalytic features compared to their lower mismatch counterparts under the same high-temperature conditions.
generation.baseline: Nanoparticles with moderate atomic size differences (and lower lattice distortion and configurational entropy) synthesized under the same conditions.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis applies to systems where nanoparticles have been synthesized as uniform solid solutions. In cases where the initial material already exhibits significant phase segregation or when extrinsic factors like oxidizing conditions dominate, different stability mechanisms may prevail.
generation.uncertainty: The quantitative thresholds (e.g., exact degree of lattice distortion, temperature limits) remain uncertain due to the interplay of factors such as surface energy effects and potential minor oxidizing influences. Further detailed experiments are required to delineate these parameters.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of near-equiatomic nanoparticles: one set with high atomic size mismatch (maximized lattice distortion) and a second set with reduced mismatch. Subject both sets to prolonged thermal cycling within the service-relevant temperature range (773–1173 K for catalytic applications) in an inert atmosphere. Characterize before and after treatment using TEM for morphology, XRD for phase composition, and EDS mapping for elemental distribution.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If both nanoparticle sets exhibit comparable levels of phase segregation, coarsening, or loss of catalytic activity despite differing degrees of lattice distortion, then the proposed role of severe lattice distortion (in conjunction with high configurational entropy) in stabilizing the nanoparticles is invalidated.

cited_evidence.text: High-entropy alloys (HEAs) have attracted much attention in various fields with regard to applications as structural materials, biomaterials, supercapacitors, and catalysts., HEAs comprise mixtures of five or more metallic elements at near equiatomic ratios and form simple single solid-solution phases having lattice structures including face-centered cubic (fcc) and body-centered cubic (bcc)., The high configurational entropy of these alloys stabilizes the solid-solution phase such that this phase appears rather than an intermetallic phase or phase segregation., The severe lattice distortion in these materials that results from differences in the atomic sizes of the constituent elements also causes low atomic diffusivity. The unique synergistic effects resulting from combining multiple elements provide high specific strength, ductility, corrosion resistance, and thermal stability, such that HEAs are unique and fascinating materials. In recent years, many researchers have reported that HEA nanoparticles (NPs) having sizes on the nanometer scale (that is, in the range of 1 to 100 nm) show promise with regard to catalytic applications. Since the successful fabrication of the first-ever entropy- stabilized oxides, or, more general, high-entropy oxides (HEOs), such solid solutions have drawn much attention due to their unique compositional and structural features, namely, the extreme chemical disorder incorporated into single-crystal structures (). One representative example is that the metal ions in (Mg0.2Co0.2Ni0.2Cu0.2Zn0.2)O are unanimously divalent and randomly occupy the cationic sites in a rocksalt structure. These cations are coordinated by lattice oxygen in an octahedral configuration, even though Cu(II) and Zn(II) are usually four coordinated to oxygen atoms as, for example, in their binary oxides (). This stabilization of Cu(II) and Zn(II) in an unfavorable configuration is ascribable to the increased configurational entropy and a high solid solution temperature (, , ). Inspired by rocksalt HEOs, researchers have undertaken extensive work to develop diverse types of HEOs. HEOs in different crystal structures have been synthesized accordingly in the past decade, such as fluorite (, ), perovskite (), spinel (), bixbyite (), and pyrochlore (, ). In nanomaterial science, developing methods for the rapid and reliable synthesis of nanoparticles, especially from complex materials like HEAs, is essential [,]. HEAs, with their composition of four or more principal elements in nearly equal molar ratios, have significantly altered the traditional approach to alloy design. These alloys are distinguished by their diverse multi-element composition, leading to an array of desirable physicochemical and mechanical properties [,]. Their versatile application potential spans a range of industries, including high-temperature materials, anti-corrosion, electrocatalysis, advanced welding, and brazing [,,,,]. The real power of HEAs lies in their high-entropy effect, which promotes the formation of simple solid phases over a more intermetallic composition, thereby granting these alloys remarkable characteristics. In our study, we selected an HEA composed of CuCoMn1.75NiFe0.25 due to its potential catalytic properties stemming from its composition, its effectiveness in brazing and welding applications, and the high probability of being single phase [,,,,,].
